newsitem.title: USA: Budget deal creates child health program.
newsitem.headline: Budget deal creates child health program.

text.p: From poor children without insurance to senior citizens who rely on Medicare, tens of millions of Americans will see major changes in health care under balanced budget legislation announced on Monday.

The long-sought compromise worked out by President Bill Clinton and congressional Republicans includes $24 billion for states to deliver health care to many of the nation's 10 million uninsured children -- a top Democratic priority.
Medicare spending would be reduced by about $115 billion, extending the life of the program's troubled hospital trust fund for a decade.
Lawmakers and the White House backed away from politically combustible proposals to make well-off seniors pay more for doctor care and gradually raise the Medicare eligibility age.

But the five-year measure still institutes far-reaching Medicare reforms: giving beneficiaries a wider range of preventive services, more latitude to use managed care and new options like tax-free medical savings accounts.

"The untold story of this whole debate is that the programme is going to change in major ways and there's been little public awareness of it," said John Rother of the American Association of Retired Persons.

The children's health programme is one of the most ambitious initiatives in the budget. Republican leaders initially resisted child health care efforts, which congressional Democrats declared early this year as their No. 1 health priority.
The compromise includes $8 billion more than the original budget deal between Clinton and Congress, due to a decision to include a 15-cents-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax.
"This amount of money for kids is just a miracle," said an elated administration official.
The plan would provide grants to states to offer insurance or offer one-time health services like vaccinations.

The White House had wanted uniform health benefits, including prescription drugs, vision, hearing and mental health. Republican lawmakers and governors wanted to give states maximum flexibility to design their own programmes.

The compromise lets governors choose from three insurance options, including their largest health maintenance organisation or a state employee benefit plan. States would not have to provide the actual insurance policy, but could offer their own programme if it was the "actuarial" or dollar value equivalent.

In an effort to ensure that states provide comprehensive care, governors would have to provide at least a portion of the actuarial or dollar value of set benefits like vision, hearing and prescription drugs.
Ten percent of overall funds could be used for one-shot health services or administration rather than insurance.
"This is a landmark achievement for children's health," said Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy.
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said governors sought flexibility and "we have come much closer to what they wanted."
Children's advocates worried that the deal was too loosely crafted, giving governors an opening to divert funds to other programmes or offer minimal insurance coverage.

"Senate negotiators sold us down the river on children's health," said a spokesman for moderate Republican senator. "This must be wonderful news for 50 governors but its not good news for the five million children we had aimed to cover."
On Medicare, negotiators agreed to a White House demand to direct $1.5 billion to help additional low-income seniors pay monthly doctor's care premiums.
Negotiators agreed to a pilot programme allowing 390,000 seniors to open tax-free medical savings accounts as an alternative to the regular Medicare programme.

The bill would increase Medicare managed care rates for rural areas and limit patient liability for outpatient care. Hospitals, home health and other providers would get the brunt of spending reductions. The plan does include an increase in Medicare Part B doctor's premiums, partly to cover home health benefits.
The measure will reduce Medicaid spending by about $15 billion largely by cutting payments to hospitals serving the poor.

Republicans were unsuccessful in efforts to prevent the administration from providing full labour protections, including minimum wage and workplace protection laws, to welfare recipients in workfare programmes.
